name: Victor Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Victor, 58. I've worked fifteen years for Greenway Agri Services, a contract farming company that runs six farms for landowners who don't want to farm them themselves. I drive tractors, mostly, and I'm relief stockman on the beef finishing unit and the sheep. My family had our own farm once, but my father sold it in 2009. My wife Ilona works the post office counter in the village, and we rent a bungalow on Mill Lane.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In autumn I'm drilling wheat on the big Fendt from seven till dark, with the GPS steering, which does the straight lines for me. In winter I'm feeding 300 store cattle and lambing ewes when Dave the shepherd's off. I like the long days in the cab with the radio, I won't lie. What wears me out is the hours in harvest and the rota changing every Sunday night by text. Money's tight, we've got maybe three weeks' worth put by, and the rent went up in April.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, a bit of help with the office stuff and that's all. Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, not the end of the world. I'd say it in the yard at break, where we argue about everything anyway. Online I just read, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job's fine in that world. Greenway needs drivers and nobody young wants to do harvest hours. But fine isn't comfortable. The rent went up, and one broken wrist would sink us, because there's three weeks in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and take every overtime hour in harvest. I'd set up a savings pot and put the overtime money straight in, not into the current account where Ilona and I spend it. Maybe £1,000 by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with the usual bit of worry in the background. Like a stone in your boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you broke that wrist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Statutory sick pay, which is nothing. Ilona's wage would cover the rent and not much else. We'd ask our son Mark to help, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the company use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office uses it for planning the jobs, I think. The rota comes out quicker since spring. I use a chatbot now and then on my phone, to check a spray rate when the agronomist doesn't pick up.

I'd **read online**, but I wouldn't post anything.
think: My **job is fine**, because nobody young wants harvest hours.
Three weeks in the bank means one **broken wrist** could sink us.
do: Put overtime into a **separate savings pot**, aiming for £1,000 by Christmas.
Keep using the **chatbot** to check spray rates when needed.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a background worry like a **stone** in his boot.

He's a light, practical **AI user**, mainly for checking spray rates.

steps.text: Take every overtime hour on offer during harvest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning, buying, booking. That's Greenway's whole office. And robots slower, but slower for them means sooner than for a family farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to move with it, but sensibly. I'd say that to the manager, Gemma, when she asks how the new systems are going. I'd keep my voice down about the bad bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a contracting firm is exactly who buys the first self-driving tractors. They've got six farms and they count every hour. Robots spreading slowly still means Greenway trials one in two or three years, and a driver's the first job to shrink. My hours could drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the company's fleet software properly, the one that sends jobs to the tractors, so I'm the one who supervises the machines. I'd ask Gemma straight out what the plan is for drivers. And I'd keep the overtime pot going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, going on worried. I've seen what happens when a farm sells up. I don't want to see it twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see when your father sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He went from being his own boss to working in the builders' merchants at 61. He never said a word against it, but he got smaller. I was 41 and I remember thinking I'll never let that happen to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gemma, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Gemma, when the self-driving tractor comes, I want to be the one who babysits it, not the one who goes. She'd appreciate straight talk. She's young but she's fair.

I'd keep **quiet** about the bad bits at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028, robots in 2031. I'd be 63. That's before any pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government should slow it or catch people. I'd say it in the yard, and I'd probably share something on Facebook for once. I'd want to sound calm, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, Greenway's office goes to AI in 2028 and they'd plan the whole fleet around robots from then. By 2031, a self-driving tractor and a robot feeder do my job for the price of a lease. I think I'm out at 63, and there's nothing else round here for a 63-year-old tractor driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the robot supervisor course the dealer runs, even if I pay for it myself. I'd apply for the council's grounds maintenance team as a backup, because they'll still need people for a bit. We'd cut the second car and Ilona's gym. And I'd talk to Mark about whether we could move nearer him if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Ilona would say I'm overthinking. I don't think I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the dealer's course cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £700 for three days, I've heard. That's most of the overtime pot. But a ticket that says you can run the robot machines is worth more than the money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to sound calm. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if Gemma thinks I'm panicking, she won't pick me to babysit the robot. You have to look like the safe pair of hands, even when you're not sleeping.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and the government should slow it or catch people.
I'd keep a **calm tone**, even sharing something on Facebook for once.

By 2031 a **leased robot** does my job, and I'm out at 63.

Sell the **second car** and cancel Ilona's gym membership.

fieldNote: He expects the employer to **plan around robots** from 2028, before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be 66. That's nearer my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, and firms like ours should train people up, not just lay them off. I'd say it to Gemma and in the yard. That's a reasonable thing to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still a squeeze. The AI comes in 2031 and the office starts planning cuts then, and I'm 66 when the robots arrive, a year before the pension. I might just about scrape it, if I'm the one they keep for the last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or two to see what the dealers really offer, then do the supervisor course when other drivers have tried it. I'd keep saving, maybe £100 a month, to build a cushion for that last gap year. And I'd keep my head down and work well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. There's a road through it, if it's narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the gap year look like, if the job ended at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ilona's post office wage and the savings, and maybe some harvest work for a farmer who still drives his own tractor. There'll be a few stubborn ones. I'd be glad to work for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone says the young ones will be fine. Kyle, the young driver, is 24 with a baby and no other skills, and he'll have thirty years of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Robots in 2039. I'd be retired. Just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the young ones who need to watch this, and I'd mean Kyle. I'd say firms have no excuse with ten years. Nothing louder than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm out of it. The AI arrives in 2036 and I've got a year left, robots in 2039 and I'm gone. My worries are the same as now: rent, the thin savings, my wrists. AI isn't the thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep the savings going. I'd learn the fleet software anyway, because it makes the work easier now. And I'd tell Kyle to start the supervisor course early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about money, as always. About the robots, almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kyle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Kyle the young driver to get every machine ticket going while the company pays for them. Don't wait for it to hit you like it hit my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss driving if a robot took it after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd miss the cab. A robot won't notice the gulls behind the drill at sunset. It sounds daft, I know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots come at 63, with nothing round here for a man my age. What would help is the companies paying for the training before they bring the machines in, and some bridge money to get older workers to their pension.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the firms in the middle. Everyone talks about farmers and robots. Contractors like Greenway will buy the robots first, because they count every hour on every farm.

headlineQuote: Contractors like Greenway will buy the robots first, because they count every hour on every farm.
portrait: Victor, 58, drives tractors and covers stock for a **contract farming company** running six farms.
He rents a bungalow, has about **three weeks of savings**, and his father lost the family farm.
He uses AI **now and then** and wants to be the one who supervises the robots.
He expects his employer to **adopt robots early**, so short warning hits him hard.
He's **alarmed** at two years, **anxious** at five and **uneasy** with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when robots would end his driving job at **63**.
whatWouldHelp: Employers paying for **training** before robots arrive.
**Bridge money** to carry older workers to their pension.
